prompt: menu.html has an edit that was never staged. Ana runs git restore menu.html. What happens to the edit?
hint: Where did Git ever have a copy of it?

choices.text: It is gone, with no way back
choices.why: Right. It was never staged or committed, so Git never had a copy.

choices.text: It moves into the staging area
choices.why: That is the opposite direction. restore without --staged overwrites the working tree.

choices.text: It is saved in the reflog in case you want it back
choices.why: The reflog records commits. An edit that was never committed is not in it.

choices.text: It becomes a new commit that can be reverted
choices.why: restore creates no commit at all.

prompt: After git add menu.html, Ana runs git restore --staged menu.html. What is true afterwards?
hint: The M moved from one column to the other.

choices.text: The edit is gone from the file
choices.why: --staged only touches the staging area. The file keeps the edit.

choices.text: Only the staging area changed
choices.why: Right. The edit is still in the file. Only what the next commit would contain changed.

choices.text: The last commit is undone
choices.why: No commit is touched by restore.

choices.text: menu.html is no longer tracked
choices.why: It is still tracked; its change is simply not staged.

prompt: git show HEAD~3:menu.html and git restore --source=HEAD~3 menu.html both deal with the menu of three commits ago. What is the difference?
hint: One of them changes the disk.

choices.text: show prints; restore writes the file
choices.why: Right. After restore, git status shows menu.html as modified.

choices.text: show changes the file; restore only prints it
choices.why: The other way round. show never changes anything.

choices.text: restore also makes a commit of the old version
choices.why: It only changes the file. Committing it would be your decision.

choices.text: There is none; they are two names for one command
choices.why: One reads and one writes, which is the whole difference.

prompt: To put menu.html back as it was two commits ago: git restore ___=HEAD~2 menu.html
hint: The option names where the old version comes from.

prompt: What does git revert eadf998 do?

choices.text: Deletes eadf998 from the history
choices.why: eadf998 stays in the log. Nothing is deleted.

choices.text: Moves the branch back to before eadf998
choices.why: That is reset. revert moves the branch forward, onto a new commit.

choices.text: Adds a commit that does the opposite
choices.why: Right. The old commit stays, and the new one undoes its change.

choices.text: Restores the files to how they were at eadf998
choices.why: It undoes that one commit's change, and keeps every later one.

prompt: Bruno's copy already has the commit that took rye bread off. Why is revert safe here when reset would not be?
hint: What happens to the ids of commits after a removed one?

choices.text: revert asks Bruno's permission first
choices.why: Git asks nobody. The difference is in what each does to the history.

choices.text: It adds to the history, so both copies still agree
choices.why: Right. Removing a shared commit would give every later commit a new id in one copy and not the other.

choices.text: reset cannot move back past another person's commit
choices.why: It can, which is exactly the danger.

choices.text: revert also updates Bruno's copy automatically
choices.why: Nothing reaches Bruno until work is shared. That is lesson 7.

prompt: After git revert --no-edit HEAD~1, which of these are in git log? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The commit that was reverted
choices.why: Yes. It stays, with its reason.

choices.text: A new commit named Revert "…"
choices.why: Yes. Git wrote that message because --no-edit accepted it.

choices.text: The commit that came after the reverted one
choices.why: Yes. Revert undoes one commit and leaves the rest.

choices.text: Nothing new; the history is left exactly as it was
choices.why: A revert is a commit, so the log grows by one.

prompt: Ana amends her last commit to fix a typo in the message. What happens to its id?
hint: The message is part of what the id is computed from.

choices.text: It stays the same, since no file changed
choices.why: The message goes into the id, so a new message is a new id.

choices.text: It changes: the result is a new commit
choices.why: Right. 4edd100 was replaced by 2dcd0dd.

choices.text: It gets a suffix saying it was amended
choices.why: Ids are hashes; they have no suffixes.

choices.text: Git refuses, because the commit already exists
choices.why: Amending the last commit is allowed and common.

prompt: Match each reset mode to what it leaves you with.

pairs.right: The undone commit's changes staged, ready to commit
The changes in the working tree, not staged
No changes anywhere: the files match the commit

right_distractors: A new commit that undoes the old one

prompt: Why is git reset --hard the dangerous mode, when the commits it steps past can still be found?
hint: Think about what was never a commit.

choices.text: It deletes the commits permanently
choices.why: The commits are still reachable through the reflog.

choices.text: It also deletes the branch
choices.why: The branch stays; it only points somewhere else.

choices.text: It sends the change to the shared server
choices.why: reset is local, like every command in this lesson.

choices.text: It overwrites uncommitted edits, which nothing kept
choices.why: Right. Commits can be found again; unsaved work in the files cannot.

prompt: With no mode given, git reset uses the ___ mode.
hint: The one between soft and hard.

prompt: Three commits ago Ana made a commit that is wrong. The branch is shared with the whole team. What should she use?
hint: Shared is the word that decides it.

choices.text: git reset --hard HEAD~3, then redo the two later commits
choices.why: That rewrites commits other people already have, and gives them new ids.

choices.text: git revert on that commit
choices.why: Right. A new commit on top undoes it, and everybody's history still agrees.

choices.text: git commit --amend, since the commit is hers
choices.why: --amend replaces only the last commit, and this one is three back and shared.

choices.text: git restore, which undoes commits without rewriting them
choices.why: restore changes files and never touches commits.

hint: It is a list about HEAD.

choices.text: A list of the places HEAD has been
choices.why: Right. Each entry names a commit, so any of them can be gone back to.

choices.text: The shared history of the team
choices.why: The reflog is local and never shared.

choices.text: A log of the edits made to each file
choices.why: It records where HEAD pointed, not edits.

choices.text: A list of commits that were reverted
choices.why: Reverts are ordinary commits in the log. The reflog records moves of HEAD.

prompt: Which of these can the reflog not bring back?

choices.text: A commit replaced by --amend
choices.why: The amended-away commit is in the reflog, as commit (amend)'s predecessor.

choices.text: A commit that reset --hard stepped past
choices.why: That is exactly what the reflog recovered in this section.

choices.text: An edit discarded by git restore, never committed
choices.why: Right. Git never had a copy of it, so no list can point at it.

choices.text: The commit a deleted branch pointed at
choices.why: Its commits stay findable through the reflog after the branch goes.

prompt: Bruno lost a commit with reset --hard on his machine. Can Ana find it in her reflog?

choices.text: Yes, reflogs are shared with the team
choices.why: A reflog is never sent anywhere.

choices.text: No, it lives only on his machine
choices.why: Right. Each reflog records its own repository's HEAD. Bruno has to look in his own reflog, where it will be.

choices.text: Yes, if Bruno had already pushed it
choices.why: If it had been shared she would have the commit, but her reflog still records only her own HEAD.

choices.text: Only if they are on the same branch
choices.why: Branches do not connect reflogs across machines.

prompt: Ana ran git reset --hard and lost a commit she wanted. Put the recovery in order.
items: Find the entry that names the lost commit
Check with git log that it is back
trap: The entry has to be found before anything moves, or the numbers shift under you.

prompt: Match each situation to the command for it.
hint: Shared or not decides two of them.

pairs.left: An edit you have not committed and do not want
A commit the whole team already has
A typo in the message of the commit you just made
Two local commits you want to take back, keeping the changes

prompt: Put these from the safest to the most dangerous.
hint: One of them only changes what the next commit contains.
trap: revert changes no existing commit; reset rewrites the branch, and --hard also overwrites files.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about what is shared, one about what was never saved.

choices.text: Reset on a shared branch gives commits new ids in your copy only
choices.why: Reset does not give commits new ids; it removes them from the branch. It is rewriting a later commit that renumbers.

choices.text: Revert is safe on commits other people already have
choices.why: Yes. It only adds.

choices.text: An amended commit is a new commit with a new id
choices.why: Yes. The old one is gone from the branch and still in the reflog.

choices.text: git restore can undo a git restore
choices.why: What restore overwrote was never saved, so nothing can bring it back.

choices.text: The reflog keeps commits nothing else points at
choices.why: Yes, for weeks, which is what makes reset recoverable.
